#9495. Our Cost Price Workbook Gave Every Product Missing From a Supplier's List the Price of the Product Above It

Every January our suppliers send new price lists, and our buyers update our cost prices before we load them into the trading system. For one large insulation and drylining supplier they used a workbook built around 2015 and copied every year since. Our product list sat on one sheet, the supplier's new list was pasted onto another, and a VLOOKUP brought each product's new cost across by the supplier's code.

The formula left out its last argument. Without it, VLOOKUP does not look for an exact match. It assumes the first column is sorted and returns the row with the largest code that is not greater than the one it was asked for. When a code is missing, it does not show an error. It quietly returns the cost of whatever product would have sat just above it. The supplier's list was sorted by code, which is the condition approximate matching needs, so for years the workbook worked well enough to hide the problem.

In January 2025 that supplier renumbered part of its range and discontinued other lines. Two hundred and twelve of our products were not on the new list. Each one took its neighbour's cost, usually a similar product in a different size, so nothing looked absurd when a buyer scrolled down the sheet. A hundred millimetre insulation board took the cost of the fifty millimetre board. Our selling prices follow cost, and thirty eight products went out below what we paid for them.

The margin review in March found it, because the margin on that supplier's range had fallen by four points. Over nine weeks it had cost us about eighteen thousand pounds. Fourteen of our other buying workbooks used the same formula.

Every lookup now asks for an exact match, with the last argument set to FALSE or with XLOOKUP, which matches exactly unless told otherwise. A missing code now shows as an error, and a count of errors sits at the top of each sheet. Cost updates no longer go through workbooks at all. The trading system's import refuses any product it cannot match and lists every change above fifteen percent for a buyer to approve.

A lookup that cannot find an answer should say so. Anything that fills a gap with a guess will look right in exactly the places where it is wrong.

#9494. How to Delete One Record From a Parquet Table Without Rewriting Everything

Software Engineer 20+ experience in data space - Data warehousing, Business Intelligence, Cloud Computing in data engineering space and AI

Software Engineer 20+ experience in data space - Data warehousing, Business Intelligence, Cloud Computing in data engineering space and AI

Software Engineer 20+ experience in data space - Data warehousing, Business Intelligence, Cloud Computing in data engineering space and AI

A while back I wrote about a service that handles deletion requests for a large data lake, and how we kept a MySQL table from falling over under the weight of its own status updates. I left one thread deliberately unplugged at the end of that piece: how do you actually delete a record from a Hive table when the underlying files are plain Parquet or JSON, formats with no Delete DML to lean on? That's the question I want to answer here.

This isn't specific to Hive or Parquet. It applies to any storage format that doesn't support row-level DELETE natively, whatever that format happens to be in your environment. Parquet on Hive is simply the concrete case I'm going to walk through, because it's the one we actually run, and it's still extremely common. Delta and Iceberg solve this problem at the table-format level for anyone already on them, but most data lakes that have grown organically over years are sitting on something older: plain Parquet or JSON files in S3, organized into Hive partitions, with no transaction log and no built-in concept of deleting a row. A file is a file. If a record in it needs to go, something has to produce a new file without that record and make it take the old one's place.

The naive version of this is to rewrite the whole partition, or worse, the whole table, every time a deletion needs to happen. That works, technically, but it means touching enormous amounts of data you never needed to touch just to remove a handful of rows, and doing it on a timeline that doesn't scale as the volume of deletion requests grows. The real problem isn't deleting a row. It's deleting a row without turning every request into a full-table rewrite.

It's worth being upfront about where this sits relative to Delta and Iceberg, since that's the first thing anyone on those formats will ask. InMobi's engineering team wrote a good piece on this which covers the same underlying problem on plain Parquet, and lands on the same conclusion most writing on this topic does: move to a format with native delete support. That's sound advice, and if you're starting fresh or dealing with a handful of tables, it's probably the right call.

It stops being the right call, the moment "move to Delta" means migrating thousands of tables owned by dozens of different teams across a large organization. That's not a setting you flip, it's a coordination problem: every team has to schedule the work, validate that downstream consumers still function against the new format, and prioritize it against everything else on their roadmap.

For a data lake with tens of thousands of existing assets, that migration is realistically a multi-year effort, and deletion requests don't pause for multi-year efforts. What follows is what we built for the tables that are in neither format today, and have no realistic path to being migrated any time soon.

There's also a second, more technical reason the deletion-vector approach isn't a full substitute even once you are migrated: a deletion vector only marks a row as deleted, the physical bytes stay in the old file until a separate compaction step runs later, which means the data isn't actually gone the moment the deletion request completes. For a regulatory deletion obligation, that gap matters on its own, independent of the migration question.

Before a table can have anything deleted from it, the team that owns it has to onboard it, and onboarding means answering two questions.

First, which column in this table maps to an index we can search by? A request comes in as something like a customer ID, and the table might store that same value under a completely different column name, customer_account_id instead of customerId, say. Every onboarded table declares that mapping up front, against a known list of valid index types we support.

Second, is the table append-only? Some tables are classic mutable datasets where existing rows can be updated or removed. Others are immutable by design, think hourly partitions of streamed event data that are written once and never touched again after that. This distinction matters enormously for how we go about finding what to delete, which is the next problem.

Parquet has no index. There's no structure telling you "the row with customerId X lives in file Y." For a mutable table, we still have to scan, there's no way around that, but we scan smart: using input_file_name(), we identify exactly which physical files within the table actually contain a matching record, rather than assuming we need to touch every file in every partition.

Immutable tables get a different treatment, because scanning the same ever-growing pile of historical partitions every single week doesn't hold up over time. For these, we run a pre-processing step we call indexing: a separate, lightweight table that just maps index_column_value to partition. Instead of scanning the whole table on every deletion cycle, we check this small index table first, get back a short list of partitions that actually matter, and only look there.

The indexing job runs as a pre-step before every deletion cycle, so it's always catching the new partitions that have accumulated since the last run. The index stays current without ever needing a full historical re-scan.

Once we know which files contain matching records, the deletion itself is narrow by design. For each affected file, we read it, filter out the rows that need to go, and write the result as a new file, abcd.parquet produces abcd_filtered.parquet. Once that filtered file is fully written, it takes over the original file's name and location, overwriting the S3 object the table actually reads from.

This is the part that makes the whole scheme safe to run without taking the table offline. An S3 object write is atomic. A reader querying the table mid-operation either sees the complete original file or the complete replacement, never anything in between. There's no partition-level lock, no window where a dashboard or another job sees a half-written or missing file. Other jobs and queries keep reading the table normally for the entire duration of the deletion run, because from their point of view, nothing is happening until the moment a file's contents change atomically underneath them.

For tables with a lot of partitions, we also parallelize the work itself. If a table has 220 partitions needing attention, we don't process them one at a time. We split the partition list into batches of fifty and run up to five parallel processes against them, four handling fifty partitions each and one picking up the remaining twenty. The targeted, file-level nature of the deletion is what makes this kind of parallel split straightforward: each batch only ever touches its own set of files, so there's no coordination needed between the parallel workers.

A deletion job that touches hundreds of partitions across parallel workers is going to fail partway through sometimes, a worker crashes, a cluster gets preempted, whatever the reason. The failure mode here is about as gentle as it gets: since the original file is never touched until the filtered replacement is completely written and ready to swap in, a crash before that point leaves the original table exactly as it was. Nothing is lost, nothing is corrupted, nothing is half-deleted.

The one cleanup responsibility we do take seriously is the staging area. Every table or partition split being processed gets its own staging location for the filtered files it's producing, and a finally block guarantees that location gets cleaned up whether the run succeeds or fails. Without that, a crashed run would leave orphaned _filtered files sitting around in S3 indefinitely, harmless to the table itself, but a quiet, creeping mess that nobody notices until someone goes looking for why a staging bucket is larger than it should be.

None of this complexity exists for its own sake. The alternative, rewriting entire partitions or whole tables on every deletion request, works at a small scale and becomes untenable at a large one. The targeted, file-level approach keeps the amount of data touched proportional to the amount of data actually changing, not to the size of the table it lives in. The indexing step for immutable tables exists for the same reason: avoiding a full historical scan every week is the difference between a deletion cycle that stays fast as the table grows, and one that gets slower every single week, forever.

The atomic swap and the finally-block cleanup are what let this run unattended, at scale, without anyone needing to watch it. Readers never see a bad state. A crash never corrupts anything. Those two guarantees are what actually make it possible to trust this as infrastructure other teams' compliance obligations depend on, not just a script that happens to work when nothing goes wrong.

One more thing worth naming directly: because the filtered file fully replaces the original in the same pass, the data is physically gone the moment a deletion run completes. There's no separate compaction or purge step waiting to happen later before the obligation is actually satisfied. For a regulatory deletion request, that's not a minor detail.

Deleting a single record from a table that was never designed to support deletion is a deceptively hard problem once you're operating at the scale of a real data lake, hundreds of partitions, formats with no native delete support, and tables that fall into genuinely different shapes depending on how they're written. The solution here isn't exotic, and it isn't a replacement for what Delta or Iceberg already do well if you're on them. It's what we built for the much larger set of tables that aren't, and won't be for a long time: know exactly which files are affected before touching anything, replace files atomically instead of in place, physically remove the data in the same pass rather than deferring it to a later compaction step, and make sure a crash leaves you with nothing worse than some cleanup work. If you've solved a similar problem on a different format or storage layer, I'd like to hear how the constraints changed your approach.

How We Stopped a Weekly Batch Job From Taking Down a Live MySQL Service

#9491. A Validation Schema for Fixed-Width Woven Carpet Takeoffs

A carpet takeoff that stores only net area cannot describe how a woven roll will be laid out. Fixed loom width, repeat dimensions, pile direction, trims, seam locations, and dye-lot boundaries all affect the information a factory needs. An estimator can produce a plausible square-meter total while still generating an unusable cut sheet.

The right output is a validated zone record. It should distinguish measured geometry, product constraints, and decisions that still require approval. ADA CARPET's specification brief is a useful field checklist for the project inputs. The schema below is an engineering recommendation, not an ADA software interface or a factory-approved calculator.

Keep four inputs apart when validating a zone.

net_geometry holds the measured carpet boundary and exclusions for stone thresholds, wet rooms, or built-in elements. weave_constraints holds the product's usable loom width, repeat dimensions, trimming allowance, and pile direction. layout_decisions holds proposed seams, pattern offsets, and transitions. release_status says whether the zone is ready for review, sample approval, or factory cutting.

This separation matters because net geometry can change without changing the weave, and a repeat can change without changing the room. If both are stored in one mutable quantity object, a design revision can silently invalidate an approved layout.

The Fairmont Peace Hotel Shanghai archive illustrates why loom width belongs in the data. ADA FLOOR records 984.4 m² of Axminster carpet, 4 m full-width weaving, 7 mm pile, 80% wool, jute backing, and 12 colors for its 2007 to 2010 restoration. That does not mean every Axminster order uses the same width. It means width was a recorded product and project constraint, not an incidental detail.

For a rectangular zone, a preliminary strip count can be derived from width and usable loom width. Real repeat synchronization and trimming still need project-specific values.

Optional fields should stay empty until they are confirmed. Filling usableLoomWidthMm with nominal loom width may ignore the actual trim allowance. Filling napDirection with a default may create offcuts that cannot share the same visual orientation. A validator should reject release when a required field is missing rather than silently supplying a convenient value.

For each proposed strip, record its nominal width, cut length, repeat offset, and dye-lot group. If an offcut is offered for reuse, validate the weave, batch, pile direction, dimensions, and approved layout before it enters the allocation. Smaller area does not automatically make an offcut suitable.

Seam validation needs more than a distance from the wall. Mark doorway swing areas, changes in finish, operable partition tracks, and other locations identified by the project team. Then compare the proposed seam coordinates with those zones.

A useful validation result is a list of conflicts and unresolved decisions rather than a single pass or fail. For example, a seam can fall outside a doorway arc but still cross a primary motif at an awkward point. That requires a drawing review, not an automatic correction.

This example is deliberately incomplete. Its dimensions are hypothetical and must not be read as an ADA CARPET project record. It demonstrates the desired behavior: the system blocks manufacturing release until product inputs and layout decisions are supplied.

A curved corridor or non-right-angle recess should not be forced into the rectangular strip formula. ADA FLOOR's supplementary archive records hand-tufted carpet in areas of InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland associated with non-right-angle boundaries and curved corridors. That record supports keeping an irregular-boundary workflow, not copying its dimensions into another project.

For an irregular zone, validate the boundary drawing revision, template or CAD source, finish transition, perimeter treatment, and physical sample. If the piece is split into sections, record the joint locations and how the pattern continues across them. A polygon area is still useful for inquiry, but it is not enough to release an irregular hand-tufted piece.

Add design revision, sample approval, and dye-lot group to the zone record. If a room is subdivided, state whether the zones share one continuous visual run. A later-phase order must not merge with an earlier phase merely because both records use the same artwork name.

Before factory release, generate a review package containing the measured boundary, strip schedule, seam plan, repeat offsets, unresolved conflicts, and linked sample approval. The factory and project team can then check the assumptions behind the quantity. A takeoff tool should make those assumptions visible. Its job is not to disguise missing product data as a precise square-meter answer.

References: ADA CARPET project specification brief and ADA FLOOR supplementary engineering archive

#9488. Seven Failed Exports Changed How I Handle Browser Capability Checks

Indie maker & YouTuber.I’m building AudienceCue, TimedSubs, and JungRoom, with more YouTube-related creator tools.

Indie maker & YouTuber.I’m building AudienceCue, TimedSubs, and JungRoom, with more YouTube-related creator tools.

Indie maker & YouTuber.I’m building AudienceCue, TimedSubs, and JungRoom, with more YouTube-related creator tools.

SubtitleGenerator renders burned-in captions in the browser. You select a local video, generate a transcript, edit the captions, and export an MP4 with the captions rendered into its frames. The video rendering runs locally in the browser.

In one session, a user received their transcript and then made seven unsuccessful attempts to export a video with burned-in captions. We observed no further events from that session.

The failure UI appended the same generic advice to the error message every time:

Your project is safe. Try again or use a current desktop Chrome browser.

When I went to find out why the exports failed, I couldn't. Our analytics sent a single hard-coded error category for every export failure, so the specific error code was thrown away at the moment of capture. There was no export table in the database, no error reporting on the export path, and the local export history only recorded successes. Other exports succeeded during the same period, so the evidence did not point to a service-wide failure.

So this article is not a root-cause story for that one session. That cause is unrecoverable. It is about the two things I could fix:

If you render, encode or package anything heavy in the browser (WebCodecs, OPFS, canvas, workers), the same two problems are probably waiting in your code.

Before letting anyone press export, the app checked this:

It checks that the APIs exist. It does not check that they work for this file at this size. VideoEncoder can exist and still refuse the codec, resolution or bitrate you need. VideoDecoder can exist and still be unable to decode the user's source.

The real capability checks did exist (can this profile be encoded, can this source be decoded, is there enough quota), but they ran after an export attempt had started. Some of them could reject the attempt before rendering began, and output verification only ran after the file was produced. Either way, the user had to spend an attempt to find out, and the UI then offered the same generic retry advice.

The fix was a small preflight that runs when the export dialog opens, before an export attempt starts. It asks four questions, in this order:

The design decision that matters most is what happens when a probe itself breaks. A probe is new code running against browser APIs that behave differently across versions and devices. If a probe throws, I can't tell whether the browser is unsupported or my probe is wrong. Blocking the user in that case would turn a bug in my checking code into a new way to stop people from exporting.

So every probe is wrapped, and a throw means "unknown", which lets the export continue:

The kernel returns a negative result for unsupported encoding, unsupported decoding, insufficient storage, or a false font result. The dialog blocks the capability failures but leaves storage shortfalls retryable, because the user can fix those.

The encode probe uses mediabunny's canEncodeVideo with the codec, resolved dimensions and bitrate of the free export profile. The decode probe opens the user's file and asks the primary video track whether it can decode.

Two scope limits are worth stating plainly:

The storage check was not new. It came from an earlier failure: during testing, a 30-minute export at 8 Mbps on a 16 GB machine ran almost to the end and then failed with QuotaExceededError when the file was finalized in OPFS. Everything before that point was wasted work.

The guard estimates the output size and compares it with the quota. The calculation below omits the surrounding fail-open error handling:

The 1.15 ratio is a safety margin for muxing overhead, not a guarantee. An estimate is not a reservation, and other tabs can use storage between the check and the render. If estimate() itself throws, the check is skipped. When I built the dialog preflight, I reused this guard instead of writing a second one.

Because low storage is fixable, it doesn't disable the export button. Once the export starts, the same check runs again, and if it still fails, the message says how much space is needed and how much is available.

During review of the first version I found a gap: probeOrFailOpen handles a probe that throws, but not one that never settles. Without a timeout, the dialog could stay stuck checking capabilities and prevent the user from starting an export at all.

The fix is a single time limit around the whole preflight:

It is important to be honest about what fail-open gives up:

I accepted those costs because the preflight's job is to catch definite, cheap-to-detect failures early. It is not a gate that has to be right every time. The runtime error handling still has to be correct on its own.

The second problem was the message. "Try again" is a promise. If a capability check rejects the requested AVC profile, immediately repeating the same attempt is unlikely to help.

The export already threw typed errors. The fix was to decide, per code, what the user should do next:

This is a policy, not a diagnosis. For three error codes, the policy removes the immediate retry action and recommends a current desktop Chrome or Edge browser. That is a suggestion, not a guarantee that another browser will succeed. The mapping also can't prove that every render-failed is temporary, so unknown errors still default to a retry.

When the preflight returns a definite "unsupported", the dialog shows a similar redirect before an export attempt starts: "This browser can't export a burned-in video. Open in a current desktop Chrome or Edge to export. Your subtitles are safe — keep editing here."

Export-failure events now also carry a six-value export_failure_kind field alongside the generic category. When an event is captured, we can see which kind of error it was, although render-failed still groups several possible causes.

The preflight kernel was written against a failing test first. Its unit tests cover the decision rules by injecting probe results:

The font case tests the kernel's rule, not the real adapter. In the app, the font adapter returns true when collection succeeds and throws when it fails, and a throw is allowed.

End-to-end tests use an injection hook, available only in test mode, that forces the encode probe to report "unsupported" or to throw. That covers both sides of fail-open in a real browser: the blocked state with its redirect copy, and the throwing probe that must not block. At a 390px viewport width, another test injects an insufficient-storage error and checks the shortfall message, a visible retry button and an enabled export button. It doesn't run a second attempt.

One gap I should name: I haven't found a test that directly asserts the eight-second timeout. The timeout is implemented, but it isn't covered the way the other branches are.

What the tests can't show is everything the probes don't cover. In a later Android investigation, export failed immediately with render-failed. On the tested phone (a Xiaomi 13 Ultra on Chrome 151), FontFaceSet.load rejected font requests that included the next/font fallback backed by local(). Loading only the primary family for export fixed that failure.

Our font preflight only collects the font resources. It doesn't run the font loading that happens later in the export path. I don't have a record of what the preflight returned on that phone, so I won't claim it passed and then failed. The point is narrower: that failure was in a step the preflight doesn't exercise. A preflight is a sample of the pipeline, not a dry run of it.

If your app does heavy work in the browser before handing something to the user, here is what I would check:

What is still unsolved: the cause of those seven failures is gone for good. Some older devices still fail at runtime in places no preflight covers yet. And a passing preflight can still end in a failed export, which is why the error mapping matters as much as the checks.

The export code described here runs in SubtitleGenerator. The lesson isn't specific to captions, though: check what you can before the expensive step, and don't ask people to retry something you already expect to fail.

#9486. Your Tests Take Twenty Minutes and You Have Stopped Running Them

When you joined, the test suite finished in about two minutes. Now it takes twenty. You still run it before you push, most of the time. But during the day you have started making several changes at once, running nothing, and hoping. When something fails, you spend an hour working out which of your six changes caused it.

Your tests are feedback, and like any feedback, it loses most of its value when it arrives late.

There is useful research on how waiting changes the way people work. Jakob Nielsen, building on a 1968 paper by Robert Miller, describes three rough limits. A tenth of a second feels instant. One second is about as long as you can wait without your train of thought breaking. At ten seconds, people start to drift off to other tasks. Twenty minutes is far beyond all three. Nobody sits and watches a suite that long, so they stop asking it questions.

That is the real cost. Not the twenty minutes, but the questions you no longer ask. Did this small change break anything? You would have checked in two minutes. You will not check in twenty.

So treat the slowness as a problem worth your time, not as weather.

Measure first. Most test tools can report which tests take longest. Often a handful of slow ones dominate the total, perhaps a few that start a real database or wait on a fixed timer.

Run less, more often. Most tools let you run only the tests for the file you are working on, or only those affected by your change. Keep the full suite for before you push and in the pipeline.

Look at the slowest tests one at a time. Can a sleep become a wait for a condition? Can a test that starts the whole application check the same thing at a lower level? Can tests run in parallel?

And raise it with your team, with numbers. The suite has gone from two minutes to twenty in a year, and here are the ten tests that cause half of it. That is a much easier conversation than the tests are slow.

A fast answer you check every few minutes is worth more than a perfect one you have stopped asking for.

#9483. High-Frequency PCB Design: 6 Practical Considerations for RF and Microwave Circuits

High-frequency PCB design introduces challenges that are not always obvious in conventional low-frequency circuit design.

As operating frequencies increase, signal behavior becomes more sensitive to material properties, transmission-line geometry, discontinuities, grounding, and fabrication tolerances.

For engineers working on RF, microwave, and high-speed electronic systems, these six areas deserve attention during the design process.

The term "high frequency" covers a broad range of applications.

A wireless communication board, an RF front-end, and a microwave circuit may have very different requirements. Define the operating frequency range and electrical targets before selecting materials or calculating trace dimensions.

These values provide a foundation for later design decisions.

Two important dielectric properties are the dielectric constant (Dk) and dissipation factor (Df).

Dk affects propagation characteristics and impedance calculations. Df describes dielectric loss.

However, engineers should avoid choosing a material based on a single headline value. Frequency dependence, test conditions, material consistency, thermal behavior, and availability also matter.

Use material data that corresponds as closely as possible to the intended operating conditions.

At high frequencies, interconnects must be treated as transmission lines rather than ideal connections.

The appropriate structure depends on the stack-up, grounding arrangement, routing constraints, and electrical targets.

Trace width alone does not determine impedance. Copper thickness, dielectric height, dielectric properties, and nearby reference conductors also contribute.

Vias, connectors, bends, and changes in transmission-line geometry can introduce impedance discontinuities.

For demanding designs, electromagnetic simulation can help evaluate transitions that are difficult to predict with simple formulas.

The PCB stack-up is an electrical design decision, not just a manufacturing detail.

Layer arrangement influences impedance, coupling, isolation, shielding, and routing flexibility.

Work through the proposed stack-up with the fabrication team early. Confirm material availability, dielectric thicknesses, copper weights, and any special fabrication constraints before finalizing the layout.

A design should have measurable acceptance criteria.

Depending on the application, verification may include:

Not every project requires every test. Select methods based on the circuit's operating range and performance requirements.

Reliable high-frequency PCB design depends on treating materials, transmission lines, stack-up, layout, and fabrication as one connected engineering problem.

Defining electrical targets early and reviewing critical transitions before production can reduce unexpected performance issues and improve communication between design and manufacturing teams.

The most useful design process is one in which electrical requirements and manufacturing constraints are evaluated together, rather than handled as separate stages.

#9482. Retargeting Has a State-Synchronization Problem

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

A prospect becomes a customer on Monday morning. On Tuesday, they see an advertisement asking them to become a customer.

The copy may be fine. The CRM may also be correct. The failure can sit between the business state, the audience pipeline, the advertising network, and the campaign configuration.

Adding better personalization will not repair a stale audience.

I would treat retargeting as a state-synchronization problem before treating it as a creative problem. The team needs to know which facts changed, where the change traveled, and what each destination can actually enforce.

A CRM status change is a business event. A segment-membership change is a derived decision. An audience update is a transmission. Network processing, identity matching, and campaign exclusion are further steps.

Each can succeed or fail independently. A correct source record does not establish that an audience was updated. A successful upload does not establish that every relevant person was matched. An available audience does not establish that the intended campaign excludes it.

HubSpot's ads-audience documentation describes audiences based on website visitors, contact segments, and other sources, with synchronization to connected networks. That is a capability description, not a promise of instantaneous suppression for every impression.

Start by drawing the actual route for one campaign. Include the authoritative business state, segment rule, connector, destination audience, and campaign setting. If nobody can name the destination exclusion, the team has not yet demonstrated suppression.

This is a bounded diagnostic task. It does not require replacing the advertising stack or moving every historical record. It requires tracing one meaningful state change through the systems already involved.

Customer is not always a sufficient suppression condition. A company may buy one product while legitimately evaluating another. A former customer may be eligible for a return campaign. A contact may belong to several companies or opportunities.

Define what the campaign is trying to avoid: acquisition ads to current customers of a specific product, ads to people without appropriate permissions, or messages inconsistent with an active commercial conversation. These are different policies.

Then identify the source facts required to apply the rule. Product ownership, active contract status, relationship scope, and approved communication eligibility may be more precise than a broad lifecycle label.

Keep the rule readable. If the only explanation is a long chain of undocumented filters, a future team will struggle to distinguish an intentional exception from a mistake.

HubSpot's segment documentation distinguishes actively maintained membership from static sets. The source choice matters when eligibility changes after an audience is first created.

A static export can be appropriate for a defined experiment or approved snapshot. It should not be assumed to follow future customer-status changes. A dynamic source can update membership, but the downstream route still needs processing and verification.

For every audience, record whether membership is a snapshot or a continuously evaluated rule. Include the source owner, rule version, refresh behavior, destination, and purpose. Mark an expired campaign's audience for review rather than leaving its origin unknown.

Also decide how removed records are represented. A pipeline that only adds new members can keep stale ones indefinitely. Updates and removals need explicit handling, not just an assumption that the next export replaces everything.

The exact behavior depends on the connector and network. Read the current documentation and inspect the available status evidence. Do not impose one platform's replacement semantics on another platform's incremental update mechanism.

Imagine a company running an acquisition campaign for a support product. A contact's associated company activates a contract. The approved policy says contacts appropriately associated with that active product relationship should leave the prospect audience and enter a customer exclusion audience.

Checkpoint one is the source decision: did the correct relationship change, and did the segment evaluate it as intended? A broad company association may be insufficient if several unrelated business units share a parent account.

Checkpoint two is transport and processing: did the connector transmit the relevant membership changes, and did the network report acceptance or an actionable error? A queued job is not a completed update.

Checkpoint three is campaign enforcement: does the running campaign use the intended exclusion in a supported way? The audience can be correct while the campaign targets another copy or omits the exclusion.

This is a constructed example, not a client incident. It illustrates why checking the CRM alone cannot explain an unwanted impression. The investigation needs evidence from each checkpoint and an honest account of what cannot be verified.

A CRM update is not an instant ad exclusion. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Google's Customer Match API guidance describes requirements for using customer data in audience workflows. Formatting, eligibility, and processing matter, but successful submission does not imply universal person-level matching.

Do not respond by collecting every possible identifier without a justified purpose and appropriate permissions. More data can increase governance risk without guaranteeing complete suppression.

Distinguish record processing from audience reach. A connector may successfully process a record while the network cannot use it as an eligible matched audience member. Reporting should not collapse those states into one synced checkbox.

Where the platform does not expose individual match results, say so. Aggregate audience status can support a bounded operational conclusion without proving that one named person will never see another acquisition ad.

Google Ads documents audience exclusions with product-specific behavior and limitations. Check the exact campaign type and current settings rather than assuming that a familiar exclusion works identically everywhere.

Audit copied campaigns, experiments, and agency-managed accounts. A correctly configured original can coexist with a later copy that uses a different audience. The customer's experience does not distinguish between the two.

Also inspect broader acquisition activity. A customer can encounter an ad through contextual or general targeting even if one retargeting route excludes them. The investigation should identify the likely delivery route before blaming the audience sync.

Do not describe all such impressions as proof of a broken connector. Some may reflect the scope of the policy or the limitations of available controls. The remedy could be a broader campaign review, a narrower claim in the creative, or acceptance of a documented residual exposure.

The important point is to stop promising perfect suppression when the system can only provide partial, conditional controls.

For a custom synchronization route, a compact audit record might retain:

These are proposed integration fields, not a claim that every connector exposes them. Store only the identifiers needed under the approved data policy. If processing status is unavailable, record that gap rather than filling it with a successful-upload timestamp. The record should help distinguish a stale source rule from a rejected removal and a campaign that never used the exclusion.

Where evidence is available, record the time of the authoritative business change, source membership evaluation, connector transmission, and destination processing. These timestamps help locate delays.

Do not subtract timestamps with different time zones or meanings without normalization. Event occurrence, ingestion, and job completion are separate moments. A source update may arrive late even when downstream processing is fast.

Report latency distributions for observable steps and keep unobservable delivery behavior separate. A pipeline processing time is not necessarily the time until the final unwanted impression. The network may not expose enough information to measure that precisely.

Track failed removals, expired snapshots, unused exclusion audiences, and campaigns referencing unexpected audience identifiers. These are actionable exceptions. A total count of synchronized contacts can look healthy while hiding the specific removals that matter.

Set review thresholds according to the campaign's risk and platform behavior. Avoid inventing a universal instant-sync service level that the integration does not promise and the business cannot verify.

A useful QA set includes a new customer, a canceled contract, an updated email address, duplicate records, and an update that fails halfway through processing. Use authorized test methods and avoid uploading unnecessary personal data.

Test retries for idempotency in custom pipelines: repeating a successful operation should not create unintended membership changes. Test removals explicitly rather than assuming that a successful add proves the whole lifecycle works.

Define a recovery path. If an exclusion update is failing, the business may choose to pause affected acquisition activity while investigating. That decision needs an owner and should reflect actual risk, not an automatic rule imposed on every minor delay.

After a repair, verify the destination state and relevant campaign configuration. A green integration panel is not sufficient evidence that the intended audience is being used.

Keep a record of unresolved limitations. Technical fixes, verified synchronization, matched audience availability, campaign enforcement, and observed customer experience are different states.

One useful review artifact is a small exception register organized by audience identifier rather than campaign nickname. Record the exact source, expected rule, destination account, last verified processing state, and campaigns that depend on it. Similar audience names can conceal different objects, especially after campaign copies and connector changes.

Keep the register focused on active risk. An abandoned test audience and a live customer-exclusion audience should not receive the same operational priority. The register should help the team repair the consequential mismatch first, not create a larger inventory that nobody uses.

AI can write a more convincing acquisition message. It cannot make that message appropriate for someone whose relationship has already changed.

The durable improvement is a traceable audience lifecycle: a precise business rule, a maintained source, explicit update and removal behavior, destination evidence, and campaign-level verification.

That architecture will not eliminate every unwanted impression. It will make the avoidable ones easier to prevent and the remaining ones easier to explain. For a customer, relevance begins with the company remembering who they are now, not who they were when an audience was first exported.

#9480. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. #9479. Rotating session encryption keys without logging everyone out

OWASP's key management guidance describes key lifecycle, cryptoperiods, separation of duties, and the need to protect keys throughout their use. NIST SP 800-57 defines a cryptoperiod as the time during which a key is authorized for use or remains in effect. [1] [2] Rotation is therefore a planned lifecycle event, not an emergency-only action.

Deploy the new key in a verify-only state first. The application should be able to decrypt old records and accept new writes under the new active key. During the overlap, new records use the new key, while old records are re-encrypted lazily or by a bounded background job. The old key remains decrypt-only until the migration completes.

Define a maximum overlap window. A permanent "old key still works" path defeats rotation. Track how many records still use each version. If a record is too old or the migration fails, the application should surface a specific error rather than silently falling back to an untracked key.

Store keys in a secret manager or hardware-backed service with access controls and audit logs. Do not put the new key in a deployment log or a chat message. Require two-person approval for production key activation when the impact is high. Test the rollback path in a non-production environment.

The old key should be destroyed only after the migration is verified and the retention period for old records has ended. Keep a sealed recovery copy if policy requires it, with an independent access path. A key that is deleted too early can make data unrecoverable; a key that is kept indefinitely keeps the compromise window open.

Test a record encrypted with the old key, a record with an unknown key version, a record with a corrupt tag, and a record written during the transition. Test a restart with only the new key active. Test a rollback to the previous configuration. The application should fail closed for invalid cryptographic data and should not log the key or the plaintext.

Monitor decrypt failures by key version and application. A sudden increase after deployment may indicate a missing key, a bad rollout, or an attempted tampering attack. Keep the alert actionable: identify the service, key version, record class, and safe remediation step.

Key rotation is complete when new writes use the new key, old data is either migrated or deliberately retired, sessions remain valid where policy requires it, and the old key has a defined destruction date. Without that final state, rotation is just a second key sitting beside the first.

[1] OWASP, "Key Management Cheat Sheet." https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Key_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

[2] NIST, "Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 - General." https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final

#9477. Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

#9474. Your AI agent marked the form accessible. It had only checked contrast.

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at thewebhig.hashnode.dev

Say you ask your AI agent to build a "request a visitor badge" form at example.com. The pull request comes back with a green line in the notes: "Accessibility: pass." The only check that ran was a contrast test on the button colours.

A single automated check was treated as a result about the whole form.

This is a fictional illustration of how Design Decision Method reports accessibility work, not a case study or a measured result. The product details below are invented for the example. It is also not a repeat of the broader handoff and evidence labels in step 6. This post is about a narrower mistake: turning one accessibility check into a claim the interface cannot support.

The docs (Release 2.2.4) already ask the agent, when it delivers the work, to label each result as proposed, heuristic review, automated check, manual test, or user research, and to say what it did not test.

The procedure on the main branch is more specific about accessibility. Its checks are prompts, not the complete standard. It asks the agent to combine automated checks with manual keyboard testing and relevant assistive-technology pairs, to record what was not tested, and to distinguish those evidence levels. If a reference file cannot be opened, the procedure on the main branch says to say so and mark the affected checks as unverified, rather than claiming them.

An honest note for the visitor-badge form might look like this:

Automated check: Contrast on the text and button colours used. No failures found. This cannot support a claim about overall accessibility. Manual test: The three fields and the submit control can be reached from the keyboard, in a logical order, with a visible focus. Tested once on a desktop keyboard. Not tested on a phone. Heuristic review: Error text for a bad host email sits next to the field (the placeholder is name@example.com). Markup only. Not tested with a screen reader. Proposed: People complete a badge request without help. Not tested. No user research. Not tested: screen reader, zoom and reflow, mobile keyboard, a native app — and web checks would not validate a native one.

Nothing in that note invents a measurement. Nothing in it claims that a standard was met.

The procedure on the main branch is direct about the limit. An automated check can support specific rule failures. It cannot support overall accessibility or usability. "Accessibility: pass" is the second kind of statement.

When the project supplies no other standard, the procedure on the main branch uses WCAG 2.2 level AA as the default web design and verification target, and says a stronger project or legal requirement wins. That is a target to design toward. It is not a result you can report from a contrast check, and the procedure on the main branch tells the agent not to claim certification, or that a standard was met, without evidence for that claim. Flag a conflict with a stronger requirement instead of quietly lowering accessibility.

The same limit applies across platforms. For native apps, the procedure on the main branch points to the platform's accessibility guidance and tools. Do not claim that web checks validate native accessibility. If example.com later needs an iOS version of the badge request, the contrast run on the website does not speak for that app.

Agents are good at running a checker and writing a confident summary. The dangerous part is the upgrade: from "these colours passed a contrast check" to "the form is accessible." Readers of the pull request cannot see the gap unless the note says what was actually tested.

The docs (Release 2.2.4) already require that gap to be visible: say what you did not test. The procedure on the main branch fills in the accessibility detail — keyboard, assistive technology, native tools, and unverified checks — so the summary cannot outrun the evidence.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee an accessible interface. What it gives you is a report that stays inside what the checks can support.

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

#9471. Space-to-Ground Connectivity: Implementing NB-NTN in Consumer Devices

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Cellular coverage ends where the map gets interesting: hiking trails, open water, disaster zones. Satellite direct-to-device fills that gap, and the first use cases are deliberately narrow: emergency SOS, remote tracking, short messaging. Narrow is fine. When someone is lost with no bars, a 160-character message to a satellite is everything.

The standard path runs through 3GPP Release 17, which adapted NB-IoT protocols for non-terrestrial networks. NB-NTN gives device makers a defined air interface instead of a proprietary one. But the standard only describes the conversation. It doesn't solve the physics of having it from a wrist.

Smartwatches are the hardest NTN platform in consumer electronics. The ground plane is tiny, the battery holds a few hundred milliamp-hours, and the antenna sits against a human body that absorbs RF for a living. Everything that follows is about those three constraints.

This article examines the physical-layer realities, RF front-end architectures, and empirical link budgets required to establish and maintain a 3GPP Release 17 NB-NTN connection directly from a wrist-worn form factor.

Standard satellite downlinks utilize Circular Polarization (typically RHCP) to eliminate Faraday rotation effects in the ionosphere and to mitigate orientation-dependent cross-polarization fading. Generating high-purity circular polarization (axial ratio < 3 dB) across a hemisphere requires either:

Dual-point fed stacked patch antennas, or

Multi-arm crossed planar inverted-F antennas (PIFAs).

In a 42-46 mm chassis  accommodating a patch antenna thick enough to achieve usable bandwidth at S-band (e.g., 3GPP Band n256: 2170–2200 MHz DL, 1980–2010 MHz UL) or L-band (Band n255: 1525–1559 MHz DL, 1626.5–1660.5 MHz UL) is physically prohibited by the Z-height consumed by the OLED panel, touch sensor, logic board, and battery.

Consequently, wearable implementations frequently make a deliberate trade-off: implement a linear (or imperfectly elliptical) radiator and accept a theoretical 3 dB polarization mismatch loss against the satellite's circular wave. Real-world axial ratios on wearable antennas typically degrade to > 8 dB off-boresight, meaning the front-end budget must explicitly absorb this 3 dB hit rather than burning PCB volume on complex phase-shifting networks

At 2 GHz, the free-space wavelength (λ) is 150 mm. A resonant half-wavelength dipole requires 75 mm. A typical watch PCB provides a continuous conductive chassis of only 30 to 40 mm (0.2λ to 0.26λ). Because the ground plane cannot support resonant return currents, the entire metal perimeter of the watch—including the exterior bezel and titanium or aluminum mid-frame—must serve as the radiator.

A common implementation is a chassis-integrated slot antenna or multi-segment inverted-F antenna (IFA) where mechanical isolation breaks in the frame act as tuning apertures. In free-space, these designs can achieve peak gains of +1 to +2 dBi. However, once placed on the body, biological loading reduces the total radiated power (TRP) and total isotropic sensitivity (TIS) significantly.

Human tissue acts as a high-permittivity capacitive load. Placing the ground plane within 82 mm of the epidermis causes two primary degradations:

Accounting for chassis limitations and body proximity, the realized on-wrist antenna gain (Gr) at low elevation angles (20° to 30°) typically falls between -3 and -6 dBi.

The defining number in NTN work is path loss: more than 160 dB between a wrist-worn device and a low-earth-orbit satellite. Every dB in that budget is contested. Antenna gain, front-end losses, and transmit power all get spent against it, and there's no margin to waste.

The power amplifier is where the budget meets the battery. The link needs enough effective radiated power to close, but the PA has to deliver it without overheating the device or draining a 300 to 500 mAh battery in minutes. PA efficiency isn't a nice-to-have here. It's the difference between a feature and a demo.

Link margin management is the operational answer. Under foliage, body blocking, or bad orientation, the device trades data rate for stability: lower-order modulation, more repetitions, narrower bandwidth. The link gets slower so it can stay alive. Designing that fallback ladder, and deciding when to climb it, is core NTN firmware work.

To evaluate feasibility, we analyze an uplink and downlink link budget for a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite at a 600 km orbital altitude, observed at a 30° elevation angle.

Slant Range and Free Space Path Loss (FSPL)

The slant distance d between the wearable terminal and the satellite is calculated as:

d = sqrt(R_E^2 * sin^2(θ) + 2 * R_E * h + h^2) - R_E * sin(θ)

FSPL = 20log10(d) + 20log10(f) + 20*log10(4π / c)

At an S-band uplink frequency of f = 2.0 GHz:

FSPL = 20log10(1.093 x 10^6) + 20log10(2.0 x 10^9) - 147.55 ≈ 159.27 dB

At S-band downlink (2.18 GHz), FSPL ≈ 160.02 dB.

The following budget reflects a 3GPP Release 17 NB-IoT NTN deployment operating with a single-tone allocation to concentrate power spectral density (PSD).

Under line-of-sight conditions with single-carrier narrowband transmission (3.75 kHz spacing), the uplink closes with a +9.94 dB margin.

However, if the user turns their body so that torso shadowing occurs (inducing an additional 10 to 15 dB attenuation), the link margin falls below zero. The modem must drop down the Modulation and Coding Scheme (MCS) ladder and engage repetition coding (N_rep = 4, 8, 16 ... 128), as standardized in 3GPP TS 36.211.

While repetitions restore the link by accumulating energy over time, they linearly scale transmit time, directly impacting the watch's battery:

Where P_DC is the DC power drawn by the PA. At +23 dBm RF output and a conservative 28% PAE, the front-end pulls approximately 714 mW. Running N_rep = 32 transitions a short transmission from a 200 ms burst into a multi-second transmission, rapidly depleting cell capacity.

LEO satellites move fast, and that motion shows up as Doppler shift. The device has to track the frequency offset continuously and compensate, or the signal slides out of the receiver's window mid-message. Doppler compensation isn't optional in NTN. It's part of the baseband's job description.

The watch's own GNSS receiver helps more than you'd expect. Position and velocity from GPS give the modem a head start on satellite acquisition and synchronization: it knows which satellite should be overhead and roughly what Doppler to expect. Sensor fusion between GNSS and the NTN stack shortens the search and saves battery.

Then there's the wrist itself. Antenna impedance changes as the wrist moves, as skin contact changes, as the strap tightens. Dynamic impedance matching adjusts the antenna tuning in real time against body loading. Without it, the carefully tuned lab performance evaporates the moment someone actually wears the device.

Validation cannot rely on standard terrestrial multipath chambers. The long propagation delays (10 to 40 ms) and dynamic orbital trajectories require specialized emulation methods.

Testing must use hand and wrist phantoms formulated to mimic human tissue dielectric properties per CTIA OTA Test Plan standards:

Relative permittivity (εr): 35 to 42 between 1.5 and 2.2 GHz.

Measurements must capture three-dimensional radiation performance:

Upper Hemisphere Total Radiated Power (UH-TRP): Quantifying total energy emitted into the skyward hemisphere (2π steradians), rather than standard total spherical integration (4π), since power absorbed by or directed through the arm does not contribute to the satellite link.

Upper Hemisphere Total Isotropic Sensitivity (UH-TIS): Evaluating the receiver's sensitivity specifically against signals originating above the artificial horizon.

Human-in-the-loop testing is the part teams underestimate. Phantom wrists, tissue-equivalent arms loaded with the device, let you measure total isotropic sensitivity and total radiated power across arm positions without booking field time. Field testing still matters, hiking trails and open sky, but the phantom catches the regressions first.

Two test dimensions deserve their own plans. The wrist-to-sky geometry changes everything: a hiker's raised arm and a runner's swinging wrist are different RF environments, and emergency use has its own posture. Multi-satellite handover testing verifies session continuity as the device moves between satellites, because a dropped session during an SOS is the failure that matters most.

SAR compliance constrains the uplink directly. High-power satellite bursts have to stay within RF exposure limits, which caps how aggressively the device can push power to close a marginal link. The regulatory team isn't a downstream reviewer here. They're a design input.

The sky-view user experience is a design problem most cellular engineers never face. The user has to orient the watch toward the satellite, which means the UI has to guide them: where to point, when the satellite passes, how long the window lasts. An SOS feature nobody can aim is a failed feature.

Battery budgeting closes the loop. Deep-sleep modes and wake-up signals have to be tuned around satellite paging latency, which is nothing like cellular paging. Every milliamp spent listening for a satellite that isn't there is battery the SOS won't have later.

The trajectory points from NB-NTN toward 5G RedCap NTN: higher bandwidth, richer wearable applications, the same physics. The antenna and link-budget disciplines don't change. The data rates do.

There's a reasonable future where satellite-to-wearable becomes a standard outdoor safety feature, as unremarkable as GPS is today. Getting there runs through the unglamorous work: antenna-chassis co-design, software-defined tuning, and validation that treats the wrist as part of the RF system.

Direct-to-satellite connectivity in a smartwatch cannot be solved through brute-force RF power scaling. Operating at the limits of battery capacity and chassis volume requires balanced physical compromises:

Closing this link demands deep co-design across mechanical packaging, structural RF, antenna tuning, and baseband firmware. Wearable NTN terminals demonstrate that even highly constrained link budgets can be made operational through targeted RF architecture and disciplined physical integration.

The watch is the smallest satellite terminal ever mass-produced. Making it work took every dB the physics allowed and a few the engineering created. That's the job.

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Traditionally, teams maintain separate implementations:

This can lead to duplicated effort and inconsistent behavior. Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) offers another approach: share suitable Kotlin code across platforms while retaining native capabilities and, when desired, native user interfaces.

This guide explains KMP from an Android developer's perspective, with architecture examples, Kotlin snippets, production considerations, real-world scenarios, and interview questions.

Kotlin Multiplatform is a technology for sharing Kotlin code across multiple platforms, including Android, iOS, desktop, and other supported targets.

You can still write Android UI with Jetpack Compose and iOS UI with SwiftUI.

The key idea: share code where it makes sense, and keep platform-specific code where it is needed.

These terms are related, but they are not interchangeable.

Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) provides the technology and project model for sharing Kotlin code across targets. It does not require sharing UI.

Compose Multiplatform is a declarative UI framework that lets you share UI code across supported platforms.

18. How do you handle platform-specific APIs?

Use expect/actual, interfaces with platform implementations, or dependency injection.

19. Can Android and iOS use different UI implementations with shared business logic?

20. What are the benefits of KMP over two independent implementations?

It can reduce duplicated business logic, improve consistency, and simplify maintenance of shared functionality.

21. How do you design Clean Architecture in KMP?

Separate presentation, domain, and data responsibilities. Keep domain logic independent of platform frameworks and inject platform implementations through abstractions.

22. How do you handle secure token storage?

Use a shared secure-storage contract with platform-specific implementations backed by Android Keystore and iOS Keychain.

23. How do you implement offline-first architecture?

Use a local database as a source of truth, record pending operations, synchronize with the backend, and handle conflicts and retries.

24. How do you manage dependency injection across platforms?

Define common dependency modules and supply platform-specific dependencies through platform modules.

Use commonTest for common logic and platform-specific tests for native integration.

26. How does iOS consume a Kotlin shared framework?

Shared Kotlin code can be compiled and exposed through an iOS-compatible framework or another supported integration mechanism. Swift consumes the exported API.

27. What is the difference between a shared repository and a platform-specific repository?

A shared repository implements common data access and business rules. A platform-specific implementation is appropriate when data access depends on native APIs or platform-specific behavior.

28. How do you manage exceptions across Kotlin and Swift?

Define clear error contracts, handle exceptions at interop boundaries, and avoid exposing implementation-specific exceptions unnecessarily.

Use an appropriate Flow-to-Swift integration strategy, such as a compatible bridge or Swift-facing wrapper. Manage collection and cancellation according to the iOS lifecycle.

30. How do you optimize KMP framework size?

Review dependencies, exported APIs, compiler configuration, and unnecessary framework exposure. Measure release binaries.

31. You have an existing Android application and want to migrate it to KMP. How would you approach it?

I would avoid rewriting the whole application.

The objective is to reduce migration risk while keeping the existing Android application stable.

32. Android works, but iOS crashes when calling a shared Kotlin API. What would you investigate?

I would investigate framework integration, Swift interoperability, nullability mapping, exception propagation, coroutine bridging, native dependencies, platform-specific implementations, and binary compatibility. I would reproduce the problem in an iOS test environment and inspect native logs.

33. Your application has 100 APIs. Should every API implementation move into commonMain?

Not automatically. I would identify which networking contracts, models, authentication rules, and repository behaviors are common. Native SDK integrations and platform-specific capabilities may remain platform-specific.

34. How would you ensure consistent offline behavior on Android and iOS?

Share data models, business rules, repository contracts, synchronization policies, and conflict resolution. Use a local source of truth, idempotent operations, and tests for concurrent updates and network interruption.

35. Your shared module has become too large. What would you do?

Organize code around business features and technical responsibilities. Introduce Gradle modules when they improve dependency boundaries, build performance, or team ownership.

36. Should networking, database, UI, and business logic all be shared?

Not necessarily. Share code according to product requirements. For an existing native application, start with domain and data logic. Evaluate shared UI separately.

37. A refresh token expires while multiple API requests are running. How would you handle it?

Centralize authentication handling in the networking layer. Coordinate refresh so concurrent requests do not independently refresh the token, retry original requests only when safe, handle refresh-token expiry, clear invalid credentials, and return an authentication-required state to the UI.

38. How would you design a KMP library for multiple applications?

Define a stable public API, keep implementation details internal, minimize platform-specific assumptions, document supported targets, provide tests, manage semantic versioning, and verify binary compatibility.

If you already know Android development, you do not need to start from zero.

The best way to learn KMP is to build a real application rather than only reading documentation.

Build one feature end-to-end before adding more features. For example, implement login across shared domain/data code and both native UIs, then add offline task creation.

Kotlin Multiplatform is valuable because it gives Kotlin developers a way to share business logic across platforms without abandoning native development.

The biggest advantage is not simply writing fewer lines of code. It is creating consistent business behavior across platforms while preserving the capabilities and user experience each platform needs.

For Android developers, a practical learning path is to start by sharing domain logic, networking, repositories, and database operations. Once you understand the architecture and native integration, explore Compose Multiplatform.

Remember: The goal of KMP is not to make Android and iOS identical. The goal is to share what should be shared and preserve what should remain platform-specific.

#9467. How much does AI actually cost? A plain-English pricing guide

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at cheyx.net

Originally published on CheyX. Written with AI assistance and fact-checked against the providers' own pricing pages and CheyX's blind-test data.

AI pricing is confusing: subscriptions, free tiers, "tokens", per-seat business plans. This guide explains all of it in plain English with real figures - and shows you the gap most people never see. Nothing here is trying to sell you a particular plan.

1. Free tiers. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity all have them. They're real and useful, with limits on volume and access to the best models. For occasional use - a few tasks a week - many people never need to pay at all.

2. Subscriptions (what most people choose). A flat monthly fee for higher limits and stronger models:

Simple, predictable - and completely disconnected from how much you actually use.

3. Pay-per-use (the API). The same underlying models, billed by the amount of text processed. This is how businesses and developers buy AI, and the unit prices are startlingly small.

API pricing is quoted per million tokens. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word, so 1 million tokens ≈ 750,000 words - about ten novels. When a price sheet says a model costs well under a dollar per million tokens, it means a full page of generated text costs a fraction of a penny. That's the entire mystery. Everything else is multiplication.

For light users, a £20/month subscription can cost many times more than the same work on pay-per-use pricing - often the difference is over £200 a year. The subscription isn't a scam - you're paying for the chat interface, memory, file uploads and zero setup. But you should know the size of the convenience fee, because for light users it's most of the bill.

See the gap for your own usage. Three plain questions - what you do with AI, how often, and how long each task is - and you'll see your real monthly cost across today's models, with live prices in your currency. Show me my savings →

Stay on a free tier if you use AI a few times a week and don't hit limits.

A subscription is right if you use AI heavily most days, want file uploads, memory, image generation and custom assistants, and the time saved is worth £18-20/month. For genuinely heavy users it's excellent value.

Pay-per-use wins if your usage is light-to-moderate or repetitive (e.g. customer replies at volume), and you - or someone technical - can spend ~30 minutes setting it up once.

Businesses: the maths gets sharper with team seats. Five Plus-style seats is ~£1,200/year; the same light usage via API can be under £50/year. At 500+ automated tasks a month, the API is almost always the right answer.

Price is only half the question. CheyX also runs blind tests where the top AIs mark each other's answers - so the calculator shows each model's quality score next to its price. See the rankings.

Subscription prices verified May-June 2026. Calculator prices update automatically. AI prices change frequently.

#9463. We ran kubectl rollout undo twice to go back two versions and the second one restored the release we had just removed

Our label service runs as a Deployment, and for years our rollback has been kubectl rollout undo. The runbook said: if a release misbehaves, undo it first and investigate after.

On a Thursday this month version 4.17 went out at ten past two. Within minutes depot printers started rejecting a share of labels, and the engineer on call ran kubectl rollout undo. The pods went back to 4.16. Errors fell but did not stop, because jobs created under 4.17 were still working through the retry queue. Seeing errors under 4.16 as well, she concluded the fault was older and ran undo again to reach 4.15. Two minutes later the error rate was back where it had started. The second undo had deployed 4.17.

A Deployment's history is a list of pod templates, one per ReplicaSet, each numbered by revision. Before the incident 4.15, 4.16 and 4.17 were revisions 29, 30 and 31. Undo without arguments means the revision before the current one. The first undo did not create anything: Kubernetes found the ReplicaSet for 4.16, scaled it back up and gave it the next number, 32, and revision 30 vanished from the history. The revision before 32 was now 31, which was 4.17, so the second undo went there and renumbered it 33. Repeated undo switches between the last two versions. It never walks further back.

kubectl rollout history would have shown 29, 31 and 32 before the second command, but the column beside the numbers was empty because nothing set a change cause, and a list of bare numbers is not something anybody reads in the middle of an incident.

We no longer roll back with undo. Our rollback script takes a version, looks up its image in our release record and sets it on the Deployment, so going back two versions means naming the version. Every release sets the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation to its version, so the history shows names, and reading it is the first step of the rollback runbook. When a release is rolled back, its retry queue is now moved to a holding queue, so errors left behind by the bad version are not mistaken for the old one's.

An undo command means whatever the tool's history means. Ours kept one copy of each version and renumbered it on every use, so undo was a switch between two states, not a step back.
